explainers.title: What Is a Border vs a Frontier?
explainers.summary: Two words people use interchangeably, but political geographers treat as opposites.
explainers.tldr: A border is a fixed, agreed line between two states. A frontier is a zone, not a line — a fuzzy edge of control that hasn't hardened into a formal boundary yet.

sections.content: A border is precise. It has coordinates, treaties, and usually a fence or a checkpoint somewhere along it. A frontier is different: it's a region, not a line. Historically, frontiers were the outer edges of a state's effective control, where authority thinned out the further you traveled from the capital. Think of the American West in the 1800s, or the Sahel before colonial mapping. Nobody could point to an exact frontier line, because there wasn't one.

Borders are legal facts. Frontiers are political processes. A government can lose a frontier gradually, through neglect or rebellion, without ever losing a border, because there was no fixed line to lose in the first place. This is why so many state-building conflicts happen in frontier zones — northern Nigeria, the Congo basin, the Afghan-Pakistan tribal areas. These are places where the state's writ runs thin long before you reach an internationally recognized line.

Most African borders were drawn as lines on a map in European capitals, often before anyone had surveyed the ground. That created a strange situation: precise borders on paper, sitting on top of what were still, in practice, frontier zones — areas no colonial or postcolonial government fully controlled. That mismatch between the legal border and the political frontier is a running theme in African state-building, and it explains why some borders are firm in law but porous in practice.

A borderland is the lived space around a border — the communities, trade routes, and family ties that straddle it, often paying little attention to which side of the line they're technically on. Borderlands can exist around even the most precisely drawn border, because a legal line doesn't erase the social and economic relationships that predate it. Understanding borderlands is often the key to understanding smuggling economies, cross-border insurgencies, and diaspora politics.

keyTerms.definition: A formally agreed, fixed line separating two states.
A zone of thinning state authority, not yet fixed into a line.
The lived, social space surrounding a border.
The practical reach of a government's authority.

explainers.title: Why Nigeria's Federalism Struggles
explainers.summary: Federalism was meant to hold Nigeria's diversity together. Here's why it keeps straining.
explainers.tldr: Nigeria's federal system was designed to balance power between a strong center and diverse regions, but heavy oil revenue centralized at the federal level has quietly turned it into federalism in name, dependency in practice.

sections.content: When Nigeria became independent in 1960, federalism was the compromise that let three very different regions — the mostly Hausa-Fulani north, the Yoruba west, and the Igbo east — join a single country without any one group feeling ruled by the others. Each region kept its own government, budget, and considerable autonomy. On paper, this was meant to be a genuine power-sharing arrangement.

The discovery of oil in the Niger Delta shifted everything. Oil revenue flows through the federal government first, then gets redistributed to states through a formula decided in Abuja. That single fact concentrated enormous power at the center, because state governments now depend on federal allocations rather than raising their own revenue. A system built to disperse power ended up funneling money — and therefore influence — upward instead.

Nigeria has split into 36 states, partly to give more groups their 'own' government, but most of these states can't fund basic operations without their monthly federal allocation. Political scientists call this fiscal federalism without fiscal autonomy: the structure of federalism exists, but the financial independence that's supposed to come with it doesn't.

sections.header: Regional grievance as a permanent feature
sections.content: Because so much depends on who controls the center, Nigerian politics often becomes a contest over federal power itself, rather than a competition of policies within a stable framework. Every region worries about being shut out of the presidency, the oil formula, or federal appointments — which is exactly the anxiety federalism was designed to prevent, not produce.

keyTerms.definition: A system dividing power between a central government and constituent states.
The division of revenue-raising and spending powers across levels of government.
The rule for sharing oil revenue between federal and state governments.
Nigeria's federal capital, shorthand for the central government.

explainers.title: The Scramble for Africa, Explained
explainers.summary: How a handful of European powers carved up an entire continent in under 20 years.
explainers.tldr: Between roughly 1881 and 1914, European powers rapidly claimed nearly all of Africa, formalizing it at the 1884 Berlin Conference — where no African representatives were present.

sections.content: Before 1880, European presence in Africa was mostly limited to coastal trading posts. Within three decades, European powers controlled almost the entire continent. This wasn't a slow drift — it was a rapid, competitive rush, driven by industrial economies hungry for raw materials and by the fear that rival powers would claim territory first.

In 1884 and 1885, representatives of European powers met in Berlin to set rules for dividing Africa among themselves, mainly to avoid war with each other over it. They agreed on principles like 'effective occupation' — you had to actually control territory to claim it, not just plant a flag. No African leaders were invited or consulted.

sections.header: Lines that ignored everything on the ground
sections.content: The borders drawn during this period paid little attention to existing kingdoms, language groups, or trade networks. Some borders split single ethnic groups across two or three colonies; others forced historic rivals into the same territory. This is the root of the mismatched-borders problem political geographers still study today.

When African countries gained independence, mostly in the 1950s and 60s, they largely kept the colonial borders rather than redrawing them — partly out of practicality, partly out of fear that reopening borders would spark endless conflict. That decision, made largely for stability, is part of why so many modern African conflicts have roots in artificial 19th-century lines.

keyTerms.definition: The rapid colonization of Africa by European powers, c. 1881–1914.
The 1884–85 meeting where European powers set rules for dividing Africa.
The principle that a colonial claim required actual territorial control.

explainers.title: What Is Balance of Power?
explainers.summary: The idea that keeps showing up whenever two or more strong states eye each other warily.
explainers.tldr: Balance of power is the idea that states act to prevent any single state from becoming powerful enough to dominate the rest — often by forming alliances against whoever is rising fastest.

sections.content: Balance of power theory says states don't just want to be strong themselves — they actively work to stop any one state from becoming so strong it can dominate everyone else. When one country's power grows too quickly, others tend to respond by building up their own strength or forming alliances against it.

In a system without a world government to enforce rules, states have to look out for their own survival. A dominant power could, in theory, ignore the interests of everyone weaker. So rational states hedge against that outcome before it happens, rather than waiting to see if a rising power turns out to be friendly.

Not every state responds to a rising power the same way. 'Balancing' means joining forces against the rising power. 'Bandwagoning' means joining the rising power instead, hoping to benefit from being on the winning side. Which strategy a state picks often depends on geography, existing alliances, and how threatening the rising power's intentions appear.

You can see balance-of-power thinking behind a lot of modern alliance-building — states forming or strengthening partnerships specifically in response to another state's growing military or economic reach. It's less a rule of physics than a recurring pattern: power that grows unchecked tends to provoke its own opposition.

keyTerms.definition: The tendency of states to counter any state that grows too dominant.
Building strength or alliances to counter a rising power.
Aligning with a rising power rather than opposing it.
An international system with no central authority above states.

explainers.title: Sovereignty: What It Actually Means
explainers.summary: One of the most-used, least-understood words in political science.
explainers.tldr: Sovereignty means a state has supreme authority over its own territory and people, and that no outside power has the right to override it — at least in theory.

sections.content: Sovereignty is the principle that a state has the final say over what happens within its own borders. No higher authority — no empire, no neighboring state, no international body — is supposed to be able to override a sovereign government's decisions about its own territory.

Political scientists split sovereignty into two parts. Internal sovereignty is a government's authority over its own population and territory. External sovereignty is recognition by other states that you're a legitimate, independent actor in the international system. A state can have one without fully having the other — think of governments that control their territory but aren't widely recognized internationally, or ones that are recognized on paper but don't fully control their own land.

In theory, sovereignty is absolute. In practice, it's constantly negotiated. International trade rules, human rights treaties, and military alliances all involve states voluntarily limiting their own freedom of action. Sovereignty hasn't disappeared, but it's rarely as total as the textbook definition suggests.

keyTerms.definition: Supreme, independent authority over a territory and its people.
A government's authority over its own population and land.
Recognition of a state's independence by other states.

explainers.title: Why Nigeria's Regions Don't Trust Each Other
explainers.summary: The north-south divide, unpacked without the usual shortcuts.
explainers.tldr: Decades of competition over federal power, uneven development, and colonial-era administrative divides have left Nigeria's regions deeply suspicious of whichever group currently holds the presidency.

sections.content: British colonial administration developed southern Nigeria's infrastructure and Western-style education earlier and more heavily than the north, partly for administrative convenience. That early gap in schools, railways, and civil service jobs shaped decades of unequal development that independence didn't automatically erase.

Because so much power and revenue flow through the federal government, control of the presidency feels existential to every region — whoever is 'in power' is seen as directing resources toward their own base. This has produced an unwritten but closely followed norm of rotating the presidency between the north and south, an attempt to manage a trust problem the constitution doesn't fully solve.

The Nigerian Civil War (1967–1970), fought after the southeastern region attempted to secede as Biafra, left a lasting scar on how regions view each other's political intentions. Even decades later, political rhetoric about marginalization or secession tends to echo — and reopen — that history.

The north is majority Muslim and the south is majority Christian, and religious identity often maps onto regional political competition, intensifying disputes that are really about resources and representation. It's rarely purely religious, but religion gives regional distrust an extra, harder-to-negotiate layer.

keyTerms.definition: The informal practice of rotating Nigeria's presidency between regions.
The secessionist state southeastern Nigeria declared in 1967, sparking civil war.
A group's sense of being excluded from power or resources.

explainers.title: Buffer States and Why They Exist
explainers.summary: Small countries that exist, in part, to keep bigger ones from touching.
explainers.tldr: A buffer state sits between two larger, rival powers, reducing the chance of direct conflict by keeping them physically apart.

sections.content: A buffer state is a smaller country positioned between two larger, often rival powers. Its presence — sometimes deliberately encouraged by the larger states — reduces the risk that the bigger powers end up sharing a direct border, which lowers the chance of accidental or opportunistic conflict.

Mongolia has long functioned as a buffer between Russia and China. Nepal and Bhutan have played a similar role between India and China. Afghanistan was treated as a buffer between the British and Russian empires during the 19th-century rivalry historians call the Great Game.

Buffer states rarely get to be neutral by choice alone — their independence is often tolerated because it suits their bigger neighbors, not because those neighbors respect it unconditionally. That leaves buffer states in a delicate position: too close to one side, and they risk alienating the other.

keyTerms.definition: A smaller state positioned between larger, rival powers.
The 19th-century strategic rivalry between the British and Russian empires over Central Asia.

explainers.title: What Is Neocolonialism?
explainers.summary: Formal independence didn't automatically mean full control — here's the theory that explains why.
explainers.tldr: Neocolonialism describes how former colonial or major foreign powers keep economic and political influence over a nominally independent country, without formally ruling it.

sections.content: When African states gained independence, they got their own flags, governments, and seats at the UN. Neocolonialism is the argument that formal independence didn't necessarily bring full control over the country's economy or major decisions, because former colonial powers and multinational companies retained deep influence.

Instead of governors and soldiers, the tools are economic: trade terms that favor the former colonizer, currency arrangements tied to a foreign central bank, loan conditions attached to major policy decisions, or foreign-owned companies controlling key resources like oil or minerals. None of this looks like colonial rule on paper, but it can shape a country's choices almost as much.

The term was popularized by Ghana's first president, Kwame Nkrumah, in the 1960s. Not every economist or political scientist agrees on how much of Africa's current economic relationships should be labeled neocolonial versus simply the ordinary asymmetries of global trade — but the concept remains a standard reference point in African politics coursework.

keyTerms.definition: Continued foreign economic or political influence over a formally independent state.
Ghana's first president, who popularized the term neocolonialism.

explainers.title: Proxy Wars: Fighting Without Fighting
explainers.summary: How major powers wage conflict against each other without their own soldiers meeting on a battlefield.
explainers.tldr: A proxy war is a conflict where major powers back opposing local sides instead of fighting each other directly, letting them compete without the cost and risk of a direct war.

sections.content: A proxy war happens when two rival powers support opposing sides of a conflict — with money, weapons, training, or intelligence — rather than sending their own troops to fight each other directly. It lets a major power pursue its strategic interests while avoiding the massive cost and risk of a direct war with a rival.

Direct war between two heavily armed states, especially nuclear-armed ones, is enormously risky. Backing a proxy allows a power to influence the outcome of a conflict, weaken a rival, or extend its own influence, all while maintaining deniability and avoiding the domestic and international backlash of open war.

The strategic calculations happen in distant capitals, but the fighting and destruction happen on the ground in the country actually at war. This mismatch — between who bears the risk and who makes the decisions — is one of the most criticized features of proxy conflicts.

keyTerms.definition: A conflict where rival powers back opposing local sides instead of fighting directly.
The ability of a power to avoid formal responsibility for its involvement.

explainers.title: What Makes a State 'Failed'?
explainers.summary: The term gets thrown around loosely — here's what political scientists actually mean by it.
explainers.tldr: A failed state is one that can no longer perform the basic functions of a state — controlling territory, providing security, or delivering services — even if it still exists on a map.

sections.content: A state is considered failed, or fragile, when its government loses the practical ability to do the things a state is expected to do: maintain a monopoly on the use of force, control its own territory, collect taxes, and provide basic services like security, courts, and infrastructure.

A failed state usually keeps its seat at the UN, its flag, and its internationally recognized borders. What it loses is functional control — armed groups, rival authorities, or sheer administrative collapse can mean the government's writ barely extends beyond the capital, even though the state still legally exists.

Critics argue the term is applied unevenly, often to poorer or non-Western states, and can oversimplify complex situations into a single blunt label. Some scholars prefer 'fragile state' or focus on specific failures — security failure, fiscal failure — rather than declaring a state failed as a whole.

keyTerms.definition: A state that has lost the practical ability to perform core state functions.

keyTerms.term: Monopoly on the use of force
keyTerms.definition: A government's sole legitimate authority to use violence within its territory.

explainers.title: Foundations of Politics
explainers.summary: The basic vocabulary and ideas that everything else in political science builds on.
explainers.tldr: Politics is how groups of people make collective decisions about power, resources, and rules when they don't naturally agree. Every other topic on this site — governments, elections, ideologies — is really just a variation on that basic problem.

sections.content: Politics is the process by which a group decides who gets power, who gets resources, and what rules everyone has to follow — especially when people disagree about the answers. Example: when a class has to pick one student representative, the campaigning, voting, and negotiating that follows is politics in miniature.

Politics exists because resources are limited and people want different things. Without some process for making binding decisions, disagreements over land, money, or rules would have to be settled by force every time. Example: two farming communities sharing one river need a political process to decide water use, or they risk constant conflict.

Politics lets societies resolve conflict, allocate resources, and coordinate large groups of people without everyone fighting it out individually. Example: Nigeria's annual national budget is a political process that decides how oil revenue gets split between roads, schools, healthcare, and defense.

Politics happens at different scales and in different arenas: domestic politics (within one country), international politics (between countries), formal politics (elections, laws), and informal politics (workplace or family power dynamics). Example: a labor union negotiating with a company is politics, even though no government is directly involved.

Power is the raw ability to make others act a certain way. Authority is power that people accept as legitimate and rightful. Example: a police officer directing traffic has authority — people obey because the role is recognized as legitimate, not just because the officer is physically strong.

Government is the set of institutions — the presidency, legislature, courts — that actually implement decisions. Politics is the ongoing contest and negotiation over which decisions get made. Example: the Nigerian government is the presidency and National Assembly; politics is the campaigning, lobbying, and debate that happens before a bill becomes law.

A state is a political and legal entity with defined territory and sovereignty. A nation is a group of people who share an identity, culture, or history — with or without their own state. Country is the everyday word covering both. Example: the Kurds are widely described as a nation, but they don't have their own internationally recognized state.

Citizenship is legal membership in a state, carrying both rights (like voting) and duties (like paying tax or obeying the law). Civic responsibility is the informal expectation that citizens participate constructively in public life. Example: paying income tax is a civic responsibility that funds public schools and roads.

Political participation is any activity aimed at influencing government or public decisions — voting, protesting, joining a party, running for office, or even just discussing politics publicly. Example: a university student union election is a small-scale but real form of political participation.

Political culture is the shared set of attitudes, values, and expectations a society holds about political life — how much people trust government, how they expect leaders to behave, what counts as fair. Example: a political culture that deeply respects elders and traditional rulers shapes how much deference younger politicians show to older ones, even in a modern democracy.

Political socialization is the process by which people develop their political values, usually shaped by family, school, religion, and media over a lifetime. Example: someone who grew up watching political news with a parent who distrusted government often carries some of that skepticism into their own adult political views.

An ideology is a fairly coherent set of ideas about how society and government should be organized — what the state should do, how resources should be distributed, what rights matter most. Example: someone who believes the government should own major industries to reduce inequality is expressing a socialist ideology; someone who wants minimal government interference is expressing a more libertarian one.

keyTerms.definition: The process of making collective decisions about power, resources, and rules.
The raw ability to make others act in a certain way.
Power that is widely accepted as legitimate and rightful.
A political and legal entity with defined territory and sovereignty.
A coherent set of beliefs about how society and government should work.

explainers.title: Types of Government Systems
explainers.summary: From democracies to monarchies to military rule — how states organize who holds power.
explainers.tldr: Government systems differ mainly along two questions: who holds power (one person, a group, or the people), and how power is structured (concentrated centrally, or split between center and regions). Almost every real-world government is some combination of the categories below.

sections.content: Democracy is a system where political power ultimately comes from the people, usually exercised through voting. Example: Nigeria holds elections every four years for president, governors, and legislators.

In a direct democracy, citizens vote on laws and policies themselves, rather than through elected representatives. Example: Switzerland regularly holds national referendums where citizens vote directly on specific policy questions.

In a representative democracy, citizens elect representatives who make day-to-day decisions on their behalf. Example: Nigeria's National Assembly — the Senate and House of Representatives — is elected to pass laws so citizens don't have to vote on every bill themselves.

In a presidential system, the head of government (the president) is elected separately from the legislature and serves a fixed term, largely independent of it. Example: Nigeria and the United States both elect their presidents separately from their legislatures.

In a parliamentary system, the executive (usually a prime minister) is drawn from the legislature and stays in power only as long as they hold its confidence. Example: the United Kingdom's prime minister is the leader of whichever party controls Parliament.

A semi-presidential system splits executive power between an elected president and a prime minister who answers to parliament. Example: France has both a president who handles foreign policy and defense, and a prime minister who manages day-to-day domestic governance.

A monarchy is a system where a king, queen, or similar hereditary ruler holds formal authority over the state. Example: the historical Benin Kingdom in what is now southern Nigeria was ruled by an Oba with significant political and religious authority.

In a constitutional monarchy, a monarch remains head of state but their power is limited by a constitution, with an elected government handling actual governance. Example: the United Kingdom's king is head of state, but elected members of Parliament and the prime minister run the country.

In an absolute monarchy, the monarch holds nearly unchecked power over the state, with no binding constitution or elected body to limit them. Example: Eswatini (formerly Swaziland) is one of the last remaining absolute monarchies in the world.

A dictatorship is a system where one person or a small group holds total power, typically without free elections or meaningful checks. Example: Nigeria under General Sani Abacha in the 1990s functioned as a dictatorship, with power concentrated in the military head of state.

A military government is one where the armed forces directly control the state, usually after seizing power in a coup. Example: Nigeria was under military rule for much of its post-independence history, including 1966–1979 and 1983–1999.

A theocracy is a system where religious leaders or religious law directly govern the state. Example: Iran's system gives its Supreme Leader, a senior religious figure, final authority over major state decisions.

A federal system divides power between a central government and regional or state governments, each with their own constitutional authority. Example: Nigeria's federal system splits power between the federal government in Abuja and 36 state governments.

A unitary system concentrates most political power in the central government, with local or regional bodies holding only limited, delegated authority. Example: France's regional governments operate mostly within powers granted by the central government in Paris.

A confederation is a loose union of independent states that cooperate on limited shared matters — like defense or trade — while each retains its own sovereignty. Example: the early United States operated as a confederation under the Articles of Confederation before adopting a stronger federal constitution in 1789.

A one-party state legally permits only a single political party to hold power, blocking meaningful opposition. Example: China's political system is built around the Chinese Communist Party as the sole governing party.

keyTerms.definition: A system where political power ultimately derives from the people.
Division of power between a central government and regional governments.
The person who runs the day-to-day operations of the state (e.g. a PM or president).
The sudden, often forceful seizure of political power, frequently by the military.

explainers.title: Political Ideologies
explainers.summary: The major belief systems that shape what people think government should and shouldn't do.
explainers.tldr: An ideology is a coherent worldview about how society, the economy, and government should be organized. Most political disagreement — about taxes, rights, or the size of government — traces back to a handful of competing ideologies.

sections.content: Liberalism emphasizes individual rights, free markets, and limits on government power. Example: laws protecting a free press and private property rights reflect core liberal principles.

Conservatism values tradition, established institutions, and gradual rather than sudden change. Example: opposing a rapid, sweeping rewrite of a country's constitution in favor of small, incremental amendments reflects a conservative approach.

Socialism favors collective or state ownership of key industries and resources, aiming to reduce inequality. Example: a government-run, tax-funded healthcare system available to all citizens reflects socialist policy.

Communism envisions a classless, stateless society with communal ownership of production, historically pursued through single-party rule and centrally planned economies. Example: the Soviet Union's centrally planned economy, where the state controlled major industries and set production targets.

Capitalism is an economic system built on private ownership and free markets, where prices and production are driven by supply and demand rather than the state. Example: Nigeria's private banking and telecom sectors operate on capitalist principles, competing for customers and profit.

Nationalism prioritizes the interests, culture, and self-determination of one's own nation, often above international or foreign considerations. Example: independence movements across colonial Africa in the mid-20th century were driven largely by nationalist demands for self-rule.

Fascism is an authoritarian, ultranationalist ideology that typically suppresses political opposition and centralizes power around a single leader or party. Example: Mussolini's Italy in the 1920s–40s banned rival parties and glorified the state and nation above the individual.

Anarchism opposes coercive state authority altogether, favoring voluntary cooperation and self-organized communities instead. Example: worker-run collectives that managed factories and farms without central state control during the Spanish Civil War reflected anarchist principles in practice.

Libertarianism pushes for maximum individual liberty and minimal government interference, especially in the economy. Example: advocating for significantly lower taxes and fewer business regulations reflects a libertarian position.

Environmentalism prioritizes protecting ecosystems and natural resources in political and economic decision-making. Example: laws mandating a shift toward renewable energy sources are driven by environmentalist policy goals.

Populism frames politics as a struggle between ordinary people and a corrupt, out-of-touch elite, and positions its leaders as champions of the former. Example: a campaign that centers its message on 'taking power back from career politicians' is using populist framing.

Progressivism pushes for social and political reform aimed at expanding equality and rights, often challenging existing traditions or institutions to do so. Example: campaigns to expand voting access to previously excluded groups reflect progressive goals.

Zionism is the political movement supporting the establishment and continued existence of a Jewish national homeland in the historic land of Israel. Example: the 20th-century immigration movements that helped establish the modern state of Israel in 1948 were driven by Zionist organizing.

Feminism in politics advocates for legal and political equality between genders, often focusing on representation, rights, and protection from discrimination. Example: laws requiring a minimum percentage of women in parliament reflect feminist-influenced policy.

Religious political movements seek to shape law and governance according to religious doctrine, ranging from influencing specific policies to advocating full religious governance. Example: political parties or movements advocating for Sharia-based law in parts of northern Nigeria reflect this category.

keyTerms.definition: A coherent set of beliefs about how society and government should be organized.
A common way of mapping ideologies from more state intervention (left) to less (right).
A nation's right to govern itself without outside control.

explainers.title: Government Structure
explainers.summary: The three branches of government and the roles that make each one work.
explainers.tldr: Most modern governments split power into three branches — executive, legislature, and judiciary — each with distinct roles, so that lawmaking, enforcement, and interpretation of law don't all sit in the same hands.

sections.content: The executive branch is the part of government responsible for enforcing and implementing laws, headed by a president or prime minister. Example: Nigeria's executive branch is led by the President and the Federal Executive Council.

A president is the elected head of state, and in many systems also head of government, typically holding significant executive power. Example: Nigeria's president serves as both head of state and head of government.

A prime minister is the head of government in a parliamentary system, usually the leader of the majority party or coalition in parliament. Example: the UK's prime minister leads the government while the king remains head of state.
A governor is the elected head of a state or provincial government within a federal system. Example: each of Nigeria's 36 states elects its own governor.
Ministers are officials appointed to head specific government departments, such as finance, health, or education. Example: Nigeria's Minister of Finance oversees national budget and fiscal policy.

The cabinet is the group of senior ministers who advise the head of government and shape major executive decisions collectively. Example: Nigeria's Federal Executive Council functions as the president's cabinet.
Government agencies are specialized bodies created to implement specific policies or regulate specific sectors. Example: Nigeria's NAFDAC regulates the safety of food and drugs sold in the country.
The legislature is the branch of government responsible for making laws. Example: Nigeria's National Assembly is its legislature.
Parliament is a common name for the legislature, especially in parliamentary systems. Example: the UK Parliament consists of the House of Commons and the House of Lords.
Congress is the name used for the legislature in some presidential systems, most notably the United States. Example: the U.S. Congress is made up of the Senate and House of Representatives.

The Senate is typically the upper chamber of a two-chamber legislature, often representing states or regions equally regardless of population. Example: Nigeria's Senate has three senators from each state, regardless of the state's population.

The House of Representatives is typically the lower chamber of a bicameral legislature, with seats allocated based on population. Example: Nigeria's House of Representatives allocates more seats to more populous states.

The lawmaking process is the formal sequence a proposal follows to become law: drafting, committee review, debate, votes, and executive approval. Example: a bill in Nigeria's National Assembly must pass both the Senate and House before going to the president for signature.
A bill is a proposed piece of legislation that has not yet become law. Example: a 'Petroleum Industry Bill' remains a bill until it passes the legislature and is signed by the president.

An act, or law, is a bill that has completed the lawmaking process and been formally enacted. Example: Nigeria's Petroleum Industry Act became law after years spent as a bill in the National Assembly.

Committees are smaller groups within a legislature that review specific bills or oversee specific policy areas in detail before a full vote. Example: a Senate committee on finance might scrutinize a tax bill line by line before it reaches the full chamber.
The judiciary is the branch of government responsible for interpreting laws and resolving legal disputes. Example: Nigeria's judiciary is headed by the Supreme Court.
Courts are institutions where legal disputes are formally heard and decided. Example: a Nigerian High Court hears major civil and criminal cases at the state level.
Judges are officials who preside over court cases and issue legal rulings. Example: a Federal High Court judge might rule on a dispute between a state government and the federal government.

A supreme court is typically the highest court in a country's judicial system, and its rulings are usually final. Example: Nigeria's Supreme Court has the final say in interpreting the Nigerian constitution.

Constitutional courts are specialized courts, found in some countries, focused specifically on whether laws or government actions comply with the constitution. Example: Germany's Federal Constitutional Court can strike down laws it finds unconstitutional.

Judicial review is the power of courts to examine, and potentially overturn, laws or government actions that conflict with the constitution. Example: a Nigerian court striking down a law found to violate constitutionally protected rights is exercising judicial review.

keyTerms.definition: The part of government responsible for enforcing and implementing laws.
A legislature made up of two chambers, such as a Senate and a House of Representatives.
A court's power to overturn laws or actions that violate the constitution.

explainers.title: Political Institutions
explainers.summary: The bodies — beyond the three main branches — that keep a political system running day to day.
explainers.tldr: Beyond the executive, legislature, and judiciary, a functioning state relies on a set of supporting institutions — electoral bodies, the civil service, security agencies, and more — that keep government running regardless of who's in office.

sections.content: An electoral commission is an independent body responsible for organizing and overseeing elections. Example: Nigeria's Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) manages voter registration and vote counting.
Political parties are organizations that field candidates for office and campaign around a shared set of policies or ideology. Example: Nigeria's APC and PDP are two of its major political parties.

The civil service is the body of permanent, non-elected officials who run government departments and implement policy regardless of which party is in power. Example: a Nigerian civil servant in the Ministry of Education keeps their job across different administrations.

This refers to the extent to which a country's armed forces shape political outcomes, formally or informally, even outside of direct military rule. Example: in some countries, the military retains informal influence over major national security decisions even under civilian government.

This covers the relationship between law enforcement and political power, including how policing can be used to maintain or challenge political control. Example: how a police force handles protests can reflect or shape a government's political priorities.

Intelligence agencies are government bodies responsible for gathering information related to national security, sometimes wielding significant political influence. Example: Nigeria's Department of State Services (DSS) handles domestic intelligence and security matters.

This covers the relationship between a country's central bank, which manages currency and interest rates, and its elected government, including how independent the bank is from political pressure. Example: the Central Bank of Nigeria sets monetary policy that is formally separate from, but can be influenced by, the presidency.

Local government is the lowest tier of government, responsible for community-level services like waste collection, local roads, and primary healthcare. Example: Nigeria's 774 Local Government Areas handle grassroots administration.

International organizations are institutions formed by multiple countries to coordinate on shared goals, from security to trade to health. Example: the African Union coordinates political and economic cooperation among African states.

keyTerms.definition: An independent body responsible for organizing and overseeing elections.
The permanent body of non-elected officials who run government departments.
The institution responsible for managing a country's currency and monetary policy.

explainers.title: Elections
explainers.summary: How elections work, the systems that decide winners, and what can go wrong along the way.
explainers.tldr: Elections are the formal process citizens use to choose leaders and representatives. The type of election, the counting system used, and the integrity of the process all shape whether the result reflects what voters actually wanted.

sections.content: Elections are the formal process by which citizens choose their representatives or leaders by voting. Example: Nigeria's 2023 general election chose a new president, governors, and legislators.
Presidential elections are held specifically to choose the office of president, usually nationwide. Example: Nigeria holds a presidential election every four years.
Parliamentary elections choose the members of a country's parliament or legislature. Example: the UK holds parliamentary elections to determine which party forms the government.

Primary elections are internal elections within a political party to choose which candidate will represent it in the general election. Example: Nigerian parties hold primaries to select their presidential candidates before the main election.

A general election is the main, nationwide election where voters choose their actual representatives from among each party's candidates. Example: Nigeria's general election determines who becomes president, governor, and legislator.

A by-election is held to fill a single seat that becomes vacant between general elections, often due to death or resignation. Example: a Nigerian state might hold a by-election if a sitting legislator dies mid-term.

First-past-the-post is an electoral system where the candidate with the most votes in a district wins, even without an outright majority. Example: Nigeria's National Assembly seats are decided by first-past-the-post in each constituency.

Proportional representation is an electoral system where parties win legislative seats in proportion to their overall vote share. Example: South Africa's National Assembly is elected through proportional representation.

Ranked-choice voting lets voters rank candidates by preference; lower-ranked candidates are eliminated and their votes reallocated until someone has a majority. Example: Australia uses a form of ranked-choice voting for its House of Representatives.
A two-round system holds a second runoff vote between the top candidates if no one wins a majority in the first round. Example: France's presidential election uses a two-round system.

Voting rights are the legal rights determining who is eligible to vote and the protections against unfair restriction of that right. Example: Nigeria's constitution grants voting rights to citizens aged 18 and older.
Voter registration is the process by which eligible citizens formally enroll to vote before an election. Example: Nigerians must register with INEC and obtain a Permanent Voter's Card to vote.

Election campaigns are the organized efforts by candidates and parties to win votes through rallies, advertising, and public appeals before an election. Example: Nigerian presidential candidates hold rallies across the country in the months before an election.

Political debates are formal public exchanges between candidates on policy and leadership, meant to help voters compare them directly. Example: a televised debate between presidential candidates lets voters compare their positions side by side.

Election monitoring is the observation of an election process by independent bodies to assess whether it was free and fair. Example: international and domestic observer groups monitor Nigerian elections for irregularities.

Election fraud is illegal manipulation of an election's outcome, such as ballot stuffing or falsifying results. Example: submitting result sheets that don't match the actual votes cast at a polling unit is a form of election fraud.

Vote buying is offering money or goods to voters in exchange for their support, undermining free choice. Example: candidates distributing cash or food items on election day to influence votes is vote buying.

Gerrymandering is the manipulation of electoral district boundaries to favor one party or group over another. Example: drawing a district's borders to concentrate opposition voters into as few districts as possible is a classic gerrymander.

Election violence is intimidation, attacks, or unrest connected to an election, aimed at influencing turnout or outcomes through fear. Example: violent clashes at polling units during an election are a recurring form of election violence.

keyTerms.definition: The set of rules used to convert votes into winners.
An electoral system where seats are allocated based on vote share.
Manipulating district boundaries to favor a particular party or group.

explainers.title: Political Parties
explainers.summary: How parties form, organize, and compete for power.
explainers.tldr: A political party is an organized group that competes for power around a shared set of goals. How a party is structured, funded, and whether it's ruling or in opposition all shape how it behaves.

sections.content: A political party is an organized group of people who share political goals and work together to win elections and hold power. Example: Nigeria's PDP is a political party built around gaining and exercising governmental power.

Parties typically form when a group with shared political goals organizes formally, often registering with an electoral commission and building structures down to the local level. Example: a new Nigerian party must register with INEC and meet requirements like having offices across a minimum number of states.

Party ideology is the underlying set of beliefs and policy positions a party claims to represent. Example: a party emphasizing free-market economics and limited government reflects a liberal or conservative ideology.

Party structure is the internal organization of a party, from national leadership down to local branches and members. Example: a party's national chairman, executive committee, and state chapters make up its structure.

The ruling party is the party currently in power, controlling the executive and often a majority of the legislature. Example: whichever party's candidate wins Nigeria's presidency becomes the ruling party at the federal level.

An opposition party is a party not currently in power, whose role includes challenging and scrutinizing the ruling party's decisions. Example: Nigeria's opposition parties critique the ruling party's policies and offer alternatives.

A coalition government forms when two or more parties join together to hold a legislative majority, usually because no single party won outright. Example: Germany is frequently governed by coalitions of two or more parties.

A party manifesto is a formal document outlining a party's policy promises and priorities, usually released before an election. Example: a manifesto might promise to build a certain number of new hospitals if the party is elected.

Party funding covers how political parties raise money to run campaigns and operate, whether through membership dues, private donations, or public funding. Example: Nigerian parties raise campaign funds partly through wealthy individual donors.

Party loyalty is the degree to which members and voters consistently support their party's positions and candidates over time. Example: a voter who always votes for the same party regardless of the specific candidate is showing strong party loyalty.

keyTerms.definition: The underlying beliefs and policy positions a party claims to represent.
A government formed by two or more parties sharing power.
A formal document laying out a party's policy promises.

explainers.title: Political Leadership
explainers.summary: The roles, styles, and expectations that define political leaders.
explainers.tldr: Political leadership spans elected officials, appointed ministers, and traditional rulers, and is judged not just by title but by legitimacy, accountability, and public trust.

sections.content: As a leadership role, the president is expected to set national direction, represent the country internationally, and often serves as commander-in-chief of the armed forces. Example: as commander-in-chief, Nigeria's president has ultimate authority over deploying troops to combat insurgency.

As a leadership role, a prime minister must maintain the confidence of parliament while managing the government's daily agenda. Example: a UK prime minister who loses a vote of confidence in Parliament can be forced to resign.

Governors are state-level leaders responsible for managing subnational government, often described as running 'mini-presidencies' within a federal system. Example: a Nigerian state governor controls the state's budget and local development projects.

Legislators are elected leaders whose core role is representing constituents' interests in lawmaking and oversight. Example: a Nigerian senator championing a bill to improve healthcare funding for their state is exercising legislative leadership.

Ministers are leaders appointed to head specific policy areas, translating broad government goals into department-level action. Example: a Minister of Works overseeing national road construction projects.

Diplomats are leaders who represent their country's interests abroad, requiring negotiation skill and cultural judgment rather than domestic political power. Example: a Nigerian ambassador negotiating trade terms with another country is exercising diplomatic leadership.
Mayors are elected leaders of cities or municipalities, focused on urban governance and services. Example: a mayor overseeing waste management and public transport within a major city.

Traditional rulers hold authority through inherited or culturally recognized status rather than election, often influential without formal constitutional power. Example: a Nigerian traditional ruler like an Emir or Oba can shape public opinion and mediate local disputes despite having no formal government role.

Leadership styles are the different approaches leaders take to exercising authority — authoritarian, consultative, transformational, and so on. Example: a consultative leader might hold town halls before major decisions, while an authoritarian leader decides unilaterally.

Good governance is leadership marked by transparency, accountability, rule of law, and responsiveness to citizens' needs. Example: a government that publishes its budget publicly and responds to citizen complaints reflects good governance.

Political accountability is the expectation that leaders answer for their decisions and can be removed or sanctioned if they fail. Example: voters holding a government accountable by voting it out after a poor economic record.

Corruption — the abuse of public office for private gain — is one of the most consistent failures of political leadership. Example: a public official diverting road construction funds into a personal account is an act of corruption.

Political legitimacy is the degree to which a leader's authority is accepted as rightful by the people they govern. Example: a leader who wins a widely recognized free and fair election typically enjoys strong legitimacy.
Public trust is the confidence citizens place in their leaders to act in the public interest. Example: repeated corruption scandals tend to erode public trust in a government over time.

keyTerms.definition: The degree to which a leader's authority is accepted as rightful.
The expectation that leaders answer for their decisions.
Leadership marked by transparency, accountability, and responsiveness.

explainers.title: Constitution and Law
explainers.summary: The legal rules that define how a state is governed and what rights citizens hold.
explainers.tldr: A constitution sets the basic rules of a political system — how power is divided, what rights citizens have, and how officials can be held to the law, even when that's inconvenient for them.

sections.content: A constitution is the foundational set of rules and principles that establishes how a state is governed and what powers and limits its institutions have. Example: Nigeria's 1999 Constitution establishes the presidency, National Assembly, and judiciary and defines their powers.

Constitutions can be written (a single formal document) or unwritten (based on tradition, statutes, and precedent), and rigid (hard to amend) or flexible (easy to amend). Example: Nigeria has a written constitution, while the UK relies on an unwritten one built from historical documents and convention.

Constitutional rights are rights guaranteed to citizens directly by the constitution, which government generally cannot override through ordinary law. Example: Nigeria's constitution guarantees the right to freedom of expression.

Separation of powers is the principle of dividing government into distinct branches — executive, legislative, judicial — to prevent any one from becoming too powerful. Example: Nigeria's presidency, National Assembly, and judiciary operate as separate branches under this principle.

Checks and balances are mechanisms that let each branch of government limit the power of the others. Example: Nigeria's National Assembly can override a presidential veto with a two-thirds majority vote.

Rule of law is the principle that everyone, including government officials, is subject to and accountable under the law. Example: a president who can be sued in court like any other citizen reflects the rule of law in action.

Human rights are basic rights and freedoms considered to belong to every person, often protected by both national constitutions and international treaties. Example: the right to be free from torture is widely recognized as a fundamental human right.

Freedom of speech is the right to express opinions and ideas without government censorship or punishment, usually with some limits, like incitement to violence. Example: a journalist criticizing government policy without fear of arrest is exercising freedom of speech.

Freedom of religion is the right to practice, change, or abstain from religious belief without government interference. Example: Nigeria's constitution protects citizens' right to practice any religion or none at all.

Due process is the legal requirement that government must follow fair procedures before depriving someone of life, liberty, or property. Example: a person accused of a crime being entitled to a fair trial before punishment reflects due process.

keyTerms.definition: The foundational set of rules establishing how a state is governed.
Dividing government into distinct branches to prevent overconcentration of power.
The principle that everyone, including officials, is subject to the law.

explainers.title: International Politics
explainers.summary: How countries interact — through cooperation, competition, and the institutions built to manage both.
explainers.tldr: International politics covers how countries pursue their interests abroad, from treaties and alliances to the global institutions — the UN, IMF, and regional blocs — built to coordinate and sometimes constrain state behavior.

sections.content: International relations is the study of interactions between countries, including diplomacy, conflict, trade, and cooperation. Example: how Nigeria manages its relationship with neighboring Niger and Chad is a matter of international relations.

Diplomacy is the practice of managing relationships between countries through negotiation rather than force. Example: two countries resolving a border dispute through talks rather than conflict is diplomacy at work.
Foreign policy is a country's overall strategy and set of goals for how it interacts with other states. Example: Nigeria's foreign policy has historically emphasized leadership in African affairs.
Treaties are formal, legally binding agreements between countries. Example: the Paris Agreement is a treaty committing signatory countries to climate action targets.
Alliances are formal partnerships between countries, often for mutual defense or shared strategic goals. Example: NATO is a military alliance among North American and European countries.

The UN is a global organization of nearly all countries, focused on maintaining peace, security, and international cooperation. Example: the UN Security Council can authorize peacekeeping missions in conflict zones.
The AU is a continental organization of African states promoting political and economic cooperation across Africa. Example: the AU has mediated peace talks in several African conflicts.

The EU is a political and economic union of European countries with shared institutions, laws, and in many cases a common currency. Example: EU member states share a single market allowing free movement of goods and people.

NATO is a military alliance of North American and European countries built around a mutual defense commitment. Example: NATO's founding principle holds that an attack on one member is treated as an attack on all.

ECOWAS, the Economic Community of West African States, is a regional bloc promoting economic integration and political stability in West Africa. Example: ECOWAS has responded diplomatically to coups in member states like Niger and Mali.

The World Bank is an international financial institution that provides loans and grants to developing countries for development projects. Example: the World Bank has funded infrastructure projects like road and power development in Nigeria.

The IMF, the International Monetary Fund, provides financial support and policy advice to countries facing economic instability. Example: countries facing a currency or debt crisis sometimes seek IMF loans, often tied to economic reform conditions.

Peacekeeping is the deployment of international forces to help maintain or restore peace in a conflict zone, typically under UN authorization. Example: UN peacekeepers have been deployed to help stabilize conflicts in places like the Democratic Republic of Congo.

International conflicts are disputes or wars between two or more countries, often over territory, resources, or ideology. Example: territorial disputes over islands in the South China Sea are an ongoing international conflict.

Sanctions are penalties imposed by one country or group of countries on another, usually economic, to pressure a change in behavior. Example: international sanctions have been used to pressure governments accused of human rights abuses.

A trade war is an escalating round of tariffs or trade restrictions between countries, usually in retaliation for each other's policies. Example: two major economies imposing rising tariffs on each other's goods is a trade war.

Global security refers to the collective concern with threats that cross national borders, like terrorism, pandemics, or nuclear proliferation. Example: international cooperation on counterterrorism intelligence-sharing is part of global security efforts.

keyTerms.definition: A country's overall strategy for interacting with other states.
A formal, legally binding agreement between countries.
Penalties, often economic, imposed to pressure a change in behavior.

explainers.title: Diplomacy
explainers.summary: The tools and people countries use to manage relationships without resorting to force.
explainers.tldr: Diplomacy is how countries negotiate, resolve disputes, and build relationships through dialogue — carried out by ambassadors, embassies, and formal agreements rather than armies.

sections.content: Diplomacy is the practice of managing relationships and resolving disputes between countries through negotiation and dialogue rather than force. Example: two countries negotiating a trade agreement instead of imposing tariffs unilaterally is diplomacy.

Ambassadors are a country's official representatives stationed in another country, responsible for maintaining relations and advancing their home country's interests. Example: Nigeria's ambassador to the United States represents Nigerian interests in Washington.

Embassies are the official offices through which a country conducts diplomacy and provides services to its citizens in a foreign country. Example: a Nigerian citizen abroad who loses their passport can seek help at the Nigerian embassy.

Diplomatic immunity is the legal protection that shields diplomats from certain laws and prosecution in the country where they're stationed, allowing them to perform their duties without local interference. Example: a diplomat generally cannot be arrested by local police for most offenses due to diplomatic immunity.
Negotiation is the process of discussing terms between parties to reach a mutually acceptable agreement. Example: trade negotiators from two countries bargaining over tariff rates.

Mediation is when a neutral third party helps two disputing sides reach an agreement without taking either side. Example: the African Union mediating peace talks between two warring factions in a conflict.

Peace agreements are formal agreements that end a conflict, often outlining terms like ceasefires, power-sharing, or territorial arrangements. Example: a peace agreement ending a civil war might include provisions for disarming rebel groups and holding elections.

International summits are formal meetings where heads of state or senior officials from multiple countries gather to discuss shared issues. Example: the G20 summit brings together leaders of major economies to coordinate on global economic policy.

keyTerms.definition: Legal protection shielding diplomats from local prosecution.
A neutral third party helping two sides reach agreement.

explainers.title: War and Conflict Politics
explainers.summary: Why wars start, how they're fought, and how they end.
explainers.tldr: Armed conflict — whether civil war, insurgency, or interstate war — is usually the product of failed politics: competing claims over power, territory, or resources that couldn't be resolved through negotiation.

sections.content: Wars typically arise from a combination of factors like competition over resources, territorial disputes, ideological conflict, or the breakdown of diplomacy. Example: disputes over control of resource-rich territory have contributed to several African conflicts.

Civil wars are armed conflicts fought between organized groups within the same country, often over control of government or territory. Example: the Nigerian Civil War (1967–1970) was fought between the federal government and the secessionist state of Biafra.

Revolutions are sudden, often forceful changes in a country's political system or leadership, driven by widespread public uprising. Example: the French Revolution overthrew the monarchy and reshaped France's entire political system.

A coup is the sudden, often forceful, seizure of political power, typically by the military or a small group within government. Example: Nigeria experienced several military coups between the 1960s and 1990s.

An insurgency is an organized rebellion against an established government, usually using guerrilla tactics rather than open warfare. Example: the Boko Haram insurgency in northeastern Nigeria has fought the government for over a decade.

Terrorism is the use of violence against civilians to achieve political goals; counterterrorism is the set of strategies governments use to prevent and respond to it. Example: Nigeria's military counterterrorism operations target Boko Haram strongholds in the northeast.

Military strategy is the planning and coordination of armed forces to achieve political or territorial objectives in a conflict. Example: a government might focus on controlling key roads and towns to isolate an insurgent group.

Peace negotiations are formal talks aimed at ending an armed conflict, often involving compromises on both sides. Example: negotiations between the Nigerian government and militant groups in the Niger Delta led to an amnesty program in 2009.

Refugee crises involve large-scale displacement of people fleeing conflict or persecution, often straining neighboring countries and international aid systems. Example: conflict in the Lake Chad Basin has driven refugee crises affecting Nigeria, Niger, Chad, and Cameroon.

keyTerms.definition: An organized rebellion against a government, usually using guerrilla tactics.
The sudden, often forceful seizure of political power.

explainers.title: Political Economy
explainers.summary: Where government decisions and economic outcomes meet — budgets, debt, taxes, and resources.
explainers.tldr: Political economy looks at how government decisions — taxation, spending, resource control — shape economic outcomes, and how economic conditions in turn shape political power.

sections.content: A government budget is the formal plan for how a government will raise and spend money over a fiscal year. Example: Nigeria's federal budget allocates funds across sectors like education, defense, and infrastructure.

Taxation policy — who pays, how much, and on what — is as much a political question as an economic one. Example: debates over raising value-added tax (VAT) in Nigeria are as much political as economic.

Public spending is government expenditure on services, infrastructure, and programs meant to benefit citizens. Example: public spending on rural electrification projects is meant to expand access to power.

National debt is the total amount of money a government owes, usually from borrowing to cover budget shortfalls. Example: Nigeria's national debt includes both domestic borrowing and loans from international lenders like the World Bank.

Rising prices directly affect political stability and government popularity, since inflation hits citizens' daily lives immediately. Example: high inflation eroding the value of wages has historically driven public discontent with Nigerian governments.

Oil politics describes the dynamics surrounding control, revenue, and distribution of oil resources, especially significant in oil-dependent economies. Example: disputes over how oil revenue is shared between Nigeria's federal government and oil-producing states are a recurring flashpoint.

Resource control is the demand, often from regions producing valuable natural resources, for greater control over and share of the revenue those resources generate. Example: Niger Delta communities have long campaigned for greater control over oil revenue generated in their region.

Economic sanctions are penalties like trade restrictions or asset freezes imposed to pressure a country's government to change its behavior. Example: sanctions have been used internationally to pressure governments involved in coups or human rights violations.

Trade policies are government rules and agreements governing how a country imports and exports goods with other countries. Example: Nigeria's participation in the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) reflects a trade policy aimed at boosting intra-African commerce.

keyTerms.definition: The total amount of money a government owes.
Demand for greater regional control over revenue from local natural resources.

explainers.title: Corruption and Governance
explainers.summary: What corruption looks like, why it persists, and how governance tries to check it.
explainers.tldr: Corruption is the abuse of public power for private gain. It thrives where institutions are weak and transparency is low — and good governance is largely the set of habits and checks that make corruption harder to get away with.

sections.content: Corruption is the abuse of entrusted public power for private gain. Example: a government official demanding a bribe to approve a legitimate business license is an act of corruption.

Corruption often stems from weak institutions, low pay for public officials, lack of transparency, and limited accountability mechanisms. Example: a poorly funded and poorly monitored government agency creates more opportunities for officials to demand bribes.

Corruption diverts public resources away from services like healthcare and education, undermines public trust, and discourages investment. Example: money meant for building a hospital being diverted into private pockets leaves communities without needed healthcare facilities.

Anti-corruption agencies are government bodies specifically created to investigate and prosecute corruption. Example: Nigeria's Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) investigates financial crimes and corruption cases.

Transparency is the degree to which government actions, especially spending and decision-making, are open and visible to the public. Example: a government publishing detailed budget information online promotes transparency.

Accountability is the principle that officials must answer for their decisions and can face consequences for wrongdoing. Example: a legislator being voted out of office after a corruption scandal reflects political accountability.

Good governance is governance characterized by transparency, accountability, rule of law, and responsiveness to citizens. Example: a local government that consults residents before major infrastructure decisions reflects good governance practices.

Misuse of public funds is the improper or illegal use of government money for purposes other than its intended, official use. Example: a public official using road-repair funds to purchase personal property is misusing public funds.

keyTerms.definition: The abuse of entrusted public power for private gain.
How open and visible government actions and spending are to the public.

explainers.title: Political History
explainers.summary: The turning points that shaped how modern political systems came to look the way they do.
explainers.tldr: Modern political systems didn't appear from nowhere — they're the product of specific historical turning points, from ancient Athens to the Cold War, each of which reshaped how power gets organized.

sections.content: Ancient Greek democracy, practiced in the city-state of Athens, was one of the earliest known forms of democracy, where eligible male citizens voted directly on laws and policies. Example: Athenian citizens gathered in an assembly to vote directly on major decisions, an early form of direct democracy.

The Roman Republic was the political system of ancient Rome before it became an empire, featuring elected officials, a senate, and checks intended to prevent any single person from gaining absolute power. Example: the Republic's system of two co-consuls sharing executive power was meant to prevent power from concentrating in one person.

The rise of modern states describes the historical process, beginning roughly in early modern Europe, by which centralized states with defined territory, sovereignty, and administrative institutions emerged. Example: the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 is often cited as a turning point establishing the modern concept of sovereign states.

This covers the political alliances, ideologies, and power struggles that shaped, and were reshaped by, the First and Second World Wars. Example: the redrawing of national borders after World War I directly shaped many political tensions that followed in Europe and the Middle East.

The Cold War was the decades-long political and ideological rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union following World War II, marked by proxy wars and a global divide between capitalist and communist blocs. Example: the rivalry played out through proxy conflicts like the Korean and Vietnam Wars, rather than direct US-Soviet combat.

The 1991 collapse of the Soviet Union saw it dissolve into 15 independent states, ending decades of Communist Party rule and the Cold War's bipolar global order. Example: countries like Ukraine and Kazakhstan became independent states following the Soviet Union's collapse.

Independence movements are political movements seeking self-rule for colonized or occupied territories, especially prominent across Africa and Asia in the mid-20th century. Example: Nigeria's independence movement led to the country gaining independence from British colonial rule in 1960.

Major revolutions are significant, often forceful, upheavals that fundamentally reshape a country's political system. Example: the French Revolution's overthrow of the monarchy fundamentally reshaped France's political structure and inspired movements elsewhere.

keyTerms.definition: The ideological rivalry between the US and Soviet Union after World War II.
A state with supreme, independent authority over its own territory.

explainers.title: Political Concepts Explained Simply
explainers.summary: A plain-language glossary of the terms that show up everywhere in political science.
explainers.tldr: These are the core vocabulary words of political science — democracy, sovereignty, legitimacy, and more — defined simply, with a real example attached to each so the definition actually sticks.

sections.content: Democracy is rule by the people, typically exercised through free and fair elections of representatives. Example: Nigeria's transition to civilian rule in 1999 marked a return to democracy after years of military government.
Sovereignty is supreme, independent authority over a territory and its people, free from outside control. Example: Nigeria's control over its own domestic laws and borders reflects its sovereignty.

A republic is a state in which power is held by the people and their elected representatives, rather than a monarch. Example: Nigeria is officially the Federal Republic of Nigeria, reflecting its elected, non-monarchical system.

A federation is a political union in which power is divided between a central government and constituent states or regions. Example: Nigeria's federation of 36 states plus the Federal Capital Territory shares power between Abuja and the states.

Liberty is the state of being free from oppressive restrictions imposed by government or others, especially concerning personal choices and rights. Example: freedom of movement, allowing citizens to travel and live where they choose, is a basic form of liberty.

Equality is the principle that all people should have the same rights, opportunities, and treatment under the law. Example: a constitution that guarantees equal protection under the law regardless of ethnicity or religion is upholding equality.

Justice is the fair and impartial treatment of individuals, especially in the application of laws and resolution of disputes. Example: a court system that treats a wealthy defendant and a poor defendant identically under the same law reflects justice.

Authority is power that is recognized as legitimate and rightful, rather than simply imposed by force. Example: an elected president's ability to issue orders that are followed because the election was seen as fair reflects legitimate authority.

Power is the raw capacity to influence or control the actions of others, with or without legitimacy. Example: a military junta holding power through force, even without an election, still has power — just not necessarily legitimate authority.

Legitimacy is the degree to which people accept a government or leader's right to hold power. Example: a government that comes to power through a widely recognized fair election typically enjoys high legitimacy.

Nationalism is a strong sense of identity and loyalty centered on one's own nation, often paired with a push for self-determination. Example: anti-colonial nationalism across Africa in the mid-20th century fueled independence movements.

Patriotism is love for and pride in one's country, often expressed through support for its institutions and symbols. Example: citizens celebrating their country's independence day is an expression of patriotism.

Propaganda is information, often biased or misleading, spread deliberately to promote a particular political agenda or point of view. Example: a government-controlled media outlet exaggerating economic success to boost public support is using propaganda.

A revolution is a fundamental and often rapid change in a country's political system, usually driven by popular uprising. Example: the Cuban Revolution of 1959 replaced the existing government with a new political system.

A coup d'état is the sudden, often forceful, illegal seizure of political power, typically by the military or a small group within the existing government. Example: Nigeria experienced several coups d'état between independence and the return to civilian rule in 1999.

Sanctions are penalties imposed by one country or international body on another to pressure a change in behavior, often economic in nature. Example: international sanctions have targeted governments accused of undermining democratic processes.

Diplomacy is the practice of managing relations and resolving disputes between countries through negotiation rather than force. Example: resolving a border dispute through talks rather than military action is diplomacy.
A treaty is a formal, legally binding agreement between two or more countries. Example: the Kyoto Protocol was a treaty committing countries to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

Negotiation is the process by which parties with different interests discuss terms to reach a mutually acceptable agreement. Example: labor unions and employers negotiating over wages is a form of negotiation, just as countries negotiate trade terms.

keyTerms.definition: Supreme, independent authority over a territory and its people.
The degree to which people accept a government's right to hold power.
The sudden, forceful, illegal seizure of political power.

explainers.title: Current Affairs
explainers.summary: How to make sense of political news as it happens, not just after the fact.
explainers.tldr: Current affairs coverage takes the concepts explained elsewhere on this site and applies them to what's actually happening right now — elections, new laws, scandals, and the 'why did this happen' behind the headlines.

sections.content: Election updates are ongoing news and analysis covering election campaigns, results, and their political implications as they unfold. Example: live coverage tracking vote counts and results as they come in on election night.
This covers news explaining major policy choices made by a government and their expected impact. Example: reporting on a fuel subsidy removal decision and its effect on transport costs.

This covers newly passed legislation and what it changes for citizens or institutions. Example: an explainer on a new data protection law and what it means for how companies handle personal information.

This covers ongoing wars, disputes, or tensions between countries and their broader implications. Example: tracking developments in an ongoing regional conflict and its effects on trade or refugee flows.
