Example: Mansa Musa is often cited by historians as possibly the wealthiest individual in history, based on the immense gold and salt resources under his control.

sections.header: A center of learning and trade
sections.content: Under Mansa Musa, Mali invested heavily in scholarship and architecture, including funding libraries and mosques in Timbuktu that made the city a renowned center of Islamic learning. Example: manuscripts from this era, some still preserved in Timbuktu, are cited today as evidence against the old myth that precolonial Africa lacked written intellectual traditions.

keyTerms.definition: The Mali Empire's most famous ruler, renowned for his extraordinary wealth.
Trade routes across the Sahara connecting West Africa to North Africa and beyond.

explainers.title: The Nigerian Civil War and the Biafra Secession
explainers.summary: How a secession attempt by Nigeria's southeast triggered one of Africa's deadliest post-independence wars.
explainers.tldr: Between 1967 and 1970, Nigeria fought a brutal civil war after the southeastern region declared independence as the Republic of Biafra, a conflict that killed an estimated one to three million people, many from famine, and still shapes Nigerian politics today.

sections.content: Following a series of violent anti-Igbo pogroms in northern Nigeria and a breakdown of trust after a 1966 counter-coup, the predominantly Igbo southeastern region, led by Lieutenant Colonel Odumegwu Ojukwu, declared independence as Biafra in 1967. Example: Ojukwu argued secession was necessary to protect Igbo lives after mass killings of Igbos living in northern Nigeria.

The Nigerian federal government fought to prevent secession, and the resulting war caused massive civilian suffering, especially through a federal blockade that led to severe famine within Biafran territory. Example: images of starving Biafran children became some of the first widely circulated humanitarian crisis photos to shape international opinion on the war.

sections.header: Federal victory and 'no victor, no vanquished'
sections.content: The war ended in 1970 with Biafra's surrender and reintegration into Nigeria, with the federal government publicly adopting a policy of 'no victor, no vanquished' aimed at reconciliation rather than punishment. Example: despite this stated policy, many Igbos and observers argue the southeast has faced lasting political and economic marginalization since the war.

The war's memory continues to shape Nigerian politics today, feeding ongoing debates about federalism, marginalization, and periodic renewed secessionist sentiment in the southeast. Example: modern pro-Biafra agitation groups explicitly invoke this history in their continued calls for southeastern independence.

keyTerms.definition: The secessionist state southeastern Nigeria declared in 1967, sparking civil war.
An organized, often violent, attack on a particular ethnic or religious group.

explainers.title: June 12, 1993: Nigeria's Annulled Election
explainers.summary: How the military annulment of a presidential election became a defining symbol of Nigeria's struggle for democracy.
explainers.tldr: On June 12, 1993, Nigerians voted in a presidential election widely regarded as free and fair, electing Moshood Kashimawo Olawale (MKO) Abiola — only for the military government to annul the results, triggering years of pro-democracy struggle that eventually led to civilian rule in 1999.

sections.content: Held under military supervision as part of a promised transition to civilian rule, the June 12, 1993 election saw MKO Abiola win a decisive victory that was broadly viewed, both domestically and internationally, as free and fair. Example: even regions outside Abiola's own political base reportedly supported him, undercutting later claims that the results were regionally biased.

Nigeria's military ruler, General Ibrahim Babangida, annulled the election results before they were formally declared, plunging the country into a political crisis and eventually leading to Babangida's own resignation shortly after. Example: the annulment was followed by a chaotic period of interim and military governments before General Sani Abacha eventually seized full power later that year.

Abiola was later arrested after declaring himself president based on his election win, and died in detention in 1998 under disputed circumstances, just as Nigeria appeared to be nearing a transition back to civilian rule. Example: Abiola's death is widely commemorated in Nigeria as a symbol of sacrifice for democracy.

sections.header: A lasting symbol of democratic struggle
sections.content: June 12 became such a powerful symbol of Nigeria's fight for democratic rule that in 2018, the Nigerian government officially renamed Democracy Day from May 29 to June 12 in recognition of the date's significance. Example: Nigeria now marks June 12 annually as a national holiday honoring this history.

keyTerms.definition: Winner of Nigeria's annulled 1993 presidential election, later a democracy icon.
Nigeria's national holiday, now marked on June 12 in honor of the annulled election.

explainers.title: Niger Delta Militancy and the Fight Over Oil Wealth
explainers.summary: How decades of pollution and unequal oil revenue sharing turned parts of the Niger Delta into an armed conflict zone.
explainers.tldr: Beginning in earnest in the 1990s and escalating through the 2000s, armed militant groups in Nigeria's oil-producing Niger Delta region attacked oil infrastructure and kidnapped workers, demanding a greater share of oil wealth and an end to environmental damage from decades of extraction.

sections.content: Decades of oil extraction brought significant environmental damage, including oil spills and gas flaring, to Niger Delta communities that saw relatively little of the resulting national oil wealth. Example: activists like Ken Saro-Wiwa campaigned against environmental damage from oil extraction in Ogoniland, and his 1995 execution by the military government drew intense international condemnation.

As peaceful activism failed to produce major change, some groups turned to armed militancy, attacking oil pipelines and kidnapping oil workers, at times cutting Nigeria's oil production significantly. Example: groups like the Movement for the Emancipation of the Niger Delta (MEND) carried out high-profile attacks on oil infrastructure in the mid-to-late 2000s.

In 2009, the Nigerian government offered an amnesty program, providing payments and job training to militants who surrendered their weapons, significantly reducing violence in the following years. Example: this amnesty program remains controversial, with critics arguing it effectively pays former militants rather than addressing the underlying grievances over resource control and environmental damage.

keyTerms.definition: Niger Delta environmental activist executed by Nigeria's military government in 1995.
Demand for greater regional control over revenue from local natural resources.

explainers.title: Nigeria's History of Military Coups
explainers.summary: How Nigeria spent more than half of its post-independence history under military rule.
explainers.tldr: Between 1966 and 1999, Nigeria experienced a series of military coups that resulted in decades of military rule, interrupted only briefly by short periods of civilian government, before a lasting transition to democracy finally took hold in 1999.

sections.content: Nigeria's first military coup in January 1966 overthrew the civilian government amid growing ethnic and regional tensions, ending the country's first attempt at post-independence democracy after just six years. Example: this coup, and a bloodier counter-coup later that year, set off the chain of events that led directly to the Nigerian Civil War.

Following the civil war, Nigeria experienced a repeating cycle of military coups and counter-coups over subsequent decades, including transitions of power among military leaders like Yakubu Gowon, Murtala Mohammed, Olusegun Obasanjo, and later Ibrahim Babangida and Sani Abacha. Example: the 1975 coup that removed Gowon happened while he was traveling abroad, a pattern repeated in several other Nigerian coups.

Nigeria did briefly return to civilian rule under the Second Republic from 1979 to 1983, before another military coup ended that democratic experiment as well. Example: this Second Republic's collapse reinforced a growing sense that Nigerian democracy remained fragile against military intervention.

sections.header: The end of the coup era
sections.content: The military era finally ended after General Sani Abacha's death in 1998, and a subsequent transition process led to Olusegun Obasanjo's election as civilian president in 1999, launching Nigeria's current, longest-running stretch of continuous civilian rule. Example: Nigeria has not experienced a successful military coup since 1999, marking a genuinely significant shift in the country's political trajectory.

keyTerms.definition: The sudden, often forceful seizure of political power, frequently by the military.
Nigeria's brief 1979–1983 return to civilian democratic rule.

explainers.title: Nigeria's Restructuring and Resource-Control Debate
explainers.summary: Why calls to redesign Nigeria's federal structure keep resurfacing in national politics.
explainers.tldr: 'Restructuring' has become a recurring buzzword in Nigerian politics, referring to a range of proposals to redistribute power and resources between the federal government and the states, driven largely by long-standing frustration over how oil revenue and political power are currently shared.

sections.content: Restructuring isn't one single specific plan — it's an umbrella term covering various proposals, from full resource control for oil-producing states to a completely reorganized regional federal system, all aimed at reducing the current concentration of power and revenue at the federal level. Example: some restructuring proposals call for returning to a regional system similar to Nigeria's early post-independence structure, rather than the current 36-state system.

A major driver of restructuring calls is the argument that oil-producing states, particularly in the Niger Delta, deserve a larger share of the revenue generated from resources extracted within their own territory. Example: current derivation formulas already give oil-producing states some additional share of oil revenue, but many argue it still falls far short of what those states experience in environmental and social costs.

Restructuring proposals face significant political resistance, partly because any redistribution of revenue or power creates clear winners and losers among Nigeria's regions, making broad political consensus difficult to achieve. Example: politicians from regions that currently benefit from the existing revenue-sharing formula have generally been more cautious about major restructuring proposals than politicians from oil-producing states.

keyTerms.definition: Proposals to redistribute power and resources within Nigeria's federal system.
The rule for sharing oil revenue between federal and state governments.

explainers.title: The Iranian Revolution of 1979
explainers.summary: How a US-backed monarchy collapsed and was replaced by an Islamic republic within a single year.
explainers.tldr: In 1979, widespread protests against Iran's US-backed monarch, the Shah, forced him into exile, and the revolution that followed replaced the monarchy with an Islamic republic led by Ayatollah Khomeini, fundamentally reshaping Iran's political system and its relationship with the West.

sections.content: Growing opposition to the Shah's authoritarian rule, perceived corruption, and close alignment with the United States fueled broad protests across Iranian society, uniting groups as different as religious clerics, secular leftists, and merchants. Example: the Shah's secret police, SAVAK, was widely feared for suppressing political dissent, fueling resentment that eventually boiled over into mass protest.

Massive protests throughout 1978 and early 1979 eventually forced the Shah to flee the country, and religious cleric Ayatollah Khomeini returned from exile to a triumphant welcome, quickly becoming the revolution's dominant leader. Example: strikes by oil workers played a major role in crippling the Shah's government's ability to function in the revolution's final months.

sections.header: An Islamic republic replaces the monarchy
sections.content: Rather than the secular or leftist government some revolutionaries had hoped for, Khomeini's faction consolidated control, establishing an Islamic republic governed under a system blending religious authority with elected institutions. Example: the new constitution created a Supreme Leader position, held by Khomeini, with authority over Iran's elected government.

The revolution transformed Iran from a close US ally into one of its most significant regional rivals, and inspired debate across the Muslim world about the viability of Islamic governance as a modern political system. Example: the US Embassy hostage crisis that followed the revolution severely damaged US-Iran relations for decades to come.

keyTerms.definition: The religious cleric who became Iran's Supreme Leader after the 1979 revolution.
A system of government where religious leaders or law directly govern the state.

explainers.title: Indian Independence and the Partition of 1947
explainers.summary: How the end of British colonial rule in India came bundled with one of history's largest, deadliest population displacements.
explainers.tldr: India gained independence from British colonial rule in 1947, but independence came paired with Partition, splitting the territory into India and Pakistan along religious lines, triggering mass displacement and communal violence that killed hundreds of thousands and displaced millions.

sections.content: Decades of nonviolent resistance, most famously associated with Mahatma Gandhi, alongside broader nationalist organizing, eventually pushed Britain to agree to Indian independence after World War II. Example: Gandhi's strategy of nonviolent civil disobedience, including the Salt March, became a globally influential model of anti-colonial resistance.

Deep tension between India's Hindu-majority and Muslim-minority populations, and fears among Muslim leaders about their political status in a Hindu-majority independent India, led to a decision to partition British India into two separate states, India and Pakistan. Example: Muhammad Ali Jinnah, leader of the Muslim League, argued that Muslims needed a separate homeland to protect their political and religious interests.

The hastily drawn partition border triggered one of history's largest mass migrations, as millions of Hindus, Muslims, and Sikhs crossed the new border in both directions, accompanied by widespread communal violence that killed hundreds of thousands of people. Example: the partition border through Punjab and Bengal was drawn so rapidly that many affected communities didn't know which country they'd end up in until after the border was announced.

The partition left India and Pakistan as rival states with unresolved territorial disputes, most notably over Kashmir, fueling ongoing tension and multiple wars between the two countries in the decades since. Example: India and Pakistan have fought several wars, largely over the status of Kashmir, since their independence in 1947.

keyTerms.definition: The 1947 division of British India into India and Pakistan.
Leader of India's nonviolent independence movement against British rule.

explainers.title: The Fall of the Berlin Wall and German Reunification
explainers.summary: How a single night in 1989 unraveled decades of Cold War division almost overnight.
explainers.tldr: The fall of the Berlin Wall in November 1989 symbolized the collapse of communist control across Eastern Europe, and within less than a year, East and West Germany, divided since the end of World War II, were formally reunified into a single country.

sections.header: A wall built to stop escape
sections.content: The Berlin Wall was built by East Germany in 1961 specifically to stop the massive flow of East Germans fleeing to the more prosperous, democratic West Germany through Berlin, becoming the most visible physical symbol of the Cold War's division of Europe. Example: East German border guards were authorized to shoot people attempting to cross the wall illegally, underscoring how seriously the East German government treated the escape problem.

Growing pro-democracy movements across Eastern Europe, combined with Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms reducing Soviet willingness to militarily enforce communist control, created an opening that East German protesters and a confused border-crossing announcement turned into a sudden, largely peaceful breach of the wall. Example: East German officials reportedly intended only a limited loosening of travel restrictions, but confused communication led crowds to simply walk through checkpoints that night.

Rather than a slow, cautious process, East and West Germany moved toward full reunification remarkably quickly, formally reuniting as a single country less than a year later in October 1990. Example: reunification required significant economic integration, since East Germany's communist-era economy was far less developed than West Germany's.

sections.header: Symbol of the Cold War's end
sections.content: The wall's fall became one of the defining symbols of the broader collapse of Soviet-backed communist governments across Eastern Europe, which continued rapidly in the months that followed. Example: several other Eastern European communist governments collapsed within months of the Berlin Wall's fall, in what's sometimes called the 'Autumn of Nations.'

keyTerms.definition: The barrier dividing East and West Berlin from 1961 until its fall in 1989.
The 1990 merging of East and West Germany into a single state.

explainers.title: The Yugoslav Wars and the Breakup of a Multiethnic State
explainers.summary: How the collapse of communist Yugoslavia unleashed a decade of ethnic conflict across the Balkans.
explainers.tldr: Following the collapse of communist rule, Yugoslavia's multiple ethnic and religious groups fought a series of brutal wars through the 1990s as the country broke apart into separate states, marked by mass killings, ethnic cleansing, and the worst atrocities in Europe since World War II.

sections.content: Yugoslavia had held together diverse ethnic and religious groups, including Serbs, Croats, and Bosnian Muslims, under communist rule, but nationalist movements gained strength as communism weakened, and the country's different republics moved toward independence at different speeds. Example: Slovenia and Croatia declared independence relatively early and with less violence than Bosnia would later experience.

The Bosnian War became the deadliest and most notorious of the Yugoslav conflicts, marked by widespread ethnic cleansing and the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, in which more than 8,000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys were killed by Bosnian Serb forces. Example: the Srebrenica massacre was later formally recognized as genocide by international courts.

After years of hesitant international response, NATO eventually intervened militarily, including airstrikes against Bosnian Serb forces and later against Serbia during the Kosovo conflict, helping bring the wars toward negotiated settlements. Example: the 1995 Dayton Agreement formally ended the Bosnian War, establishing a complex power-sharing structure between Bosnia's different ethnic groups that persists today.

The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia was established specifically to prosecute war crimes committed during these conflicts, becoming an important precedent for international war crimes accountability. Example: several senior political and military leaders from the conflicts, including Serbian leader Slobodan Milošević, were eventually put on trial for war crimes.

keyTerms.definition: The forced removal or killing of an ethnic group from a territory.
Site of the 1995 massacre later recognized as genocide during the Bosnian War.

explainers.title: The Recent Wave of Coups in the Sahel
explainers.summary: Why Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger have all seen their governments overthrown by their own militaries in just a few years.
explainers.tldr: Between 2020 and 2023, Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger all experienced military coups, driven by a mix of frustration over insurgent violence, weak governance, and growing anti-French sentiment, marking a significant reversal of the region's earlier democratic progress.

sections.content: Rather than unrelated events, this cluster of Sahel coups reflects shared regional pressures, including relentless jihadist insurgencies, weak state capacity, and public frustration that civilian governments couldn't provide basic security. Example: military officers in each country cited failure to contain insurgent violence as a primary justification for seizing power.

A significant driver has been growing public resentment toward France's continued military and political influence in its former colonies, seen by many locals as a modern extension of colonial-era control rather than genuine partnership. Example: military governments in Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger have each moved to expel French troops and diplomatic presence following their coups.

Following their coups, these governments have often pivoted toward new security partners, including Russia, and formed closer regional cooperation with each other, distancing themselves from previous Western-aligned relationships. Example: Mali's military government brought in Russian security contractors after expelling French forces.

ECOWAS has struggled to find an effective response, oscillating between threats of military intervention and eventual negotiation, while the coup governments have increasingly cooperated with each other against outside pressure. Example: Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger formed a mutual defense pact partly in response to ECOWAS pressure following their coups.

keyTerms.definition: The semi-arid region of Africa spanning from Senegal to Sudan, south of the Sahara.
An organized rebellion against a government, usually using guerrilla tactics.

explainers.title: The Israeli-Palestinian Conflict, A Basic Overview
explainers.summary: The core territorial and political dispute behind one of the world's most prolonged and closely watched conflicts.
explainers.tldr: The Israeli-Palestinian conflict centers on competing national claims to the same territory, rooted in the establishment of Israel in 1948 and the displacement of Palestinian Arabs that followed, with decades of war, occupation, and failed negotiations since.

sections.header: Competing claims to the same land
sections.content: Both Jewish and Palestinian Arab national movements developed strong historical and religious claims to the territory of historic Palestine, setting the stage for conflict once large-scale Jewish immigration and eventual statehood plans advanced in the 20th century. Example: the 1947 UN partition plan proposed dividing the territory into separate Jewish and Arab states, a plan accepted by Jewish leaders but rejected by Arab leaders at the time.

Israel's establishment in 1948 and the war that followed resulted in the displacement of hundreds of thousands of Palestinian Arabs, an event Palestinians refer to as the Nakba, or 'catastrophe,' which remains central to Palestinian political identity today. Example: many Palestinian refugee families from 1948 and their descendants still live in refugee camps across neighboring countries today.

Following the 1967 war, Israel occupied the West Bank and Gaza, territories Palestinians claim for a future state, and has since built Jewish settlements in the West Bank that most of the international community considers illegal under international law. Example: ongoing settlement expansion remains one of the most contentious issues in any renewed peace negotiations.

Multiple rounds of negotiations, including the 1990s Oslo Accords, have aimed at a two-state solution granting Palestinians their own state alongside Israel, but disputes over borders, Jerusalem, settlements, and security have repeatedly prevented a final agreement. Example: the Oslo Accords created interim Palestinian self-government in parts of the West Bank and Gaza, but were meant as a transitional step toward final status negotiations that have never successfully concluded.

keyTerms.definition: The 1948 displacement of Palestinian Arabs, central to Palestinian political identity.
A proposed resolution creating separate Israeli and Palestinian states.

explainers.title: The Syrian Civil War
explainers.summary: How a 2011 protest movement spiraled into one of the 21st century's deadliest and most internationally entangled wars.
explainers.tldr: What began as peaceful 2011 protests against Bashar al-Assad's government during the wider Arab Spring escalated into a devastating civil war involving multiple internal factions and numerous foreign powers, killing hundreds of thousands and displacing millions of Syrians.

sections.content: Peaceful protests against Assad's authoritarian government, inspired by the broader Arab Spring, were met with violent government crackdowns, which pushed parts of the opposition toward armed resistance rather than continued peaceful protest. Example: defections from Syria's military formed the core of early armed opposition groups fighting the Assad government.

The conflict grew far more complicated than a simple government-versus-opposition fight, eventually involving Kurdish forces, various rebel factions, and the extremist group ISIS, which seized significant territory in parts of Syria and Iraq at its peak. Example: ISIS's rapid territorial gains in 2014 prompted a US-led international coalition to intervene militarily specifically against the group.

Russia and Iran provided crucial military support that helped Assad's government survive, while the US, Turkey, and Gulf states backed various opposition and Kurdish factions, turning Syria into a proxy battleground for competing regional and global interests. Example: Russian airstrikes starting in 2015 were widely seen as the turning point that secured Assad's government's survival against opposition advances.

The war produced one of the largest refugee crises of the 21st century, displacing millions of Syrians internally and forcing millions more to flee to neighboring countries and beyond, straining host countries and reshaping migration politics well beyond the Middle East. Example: the resulting refugee flows into Europe starting around 2015 significantly influenced European domestic politics regarding immigration and asylum policy.

keyTerms.definition: Syria's president since 2000, whose government fought the country's civil war.
Large-scale displacement of people fleeing conflict, straining host countries and aid systems.

explainers.title: The International Criminal Court, and Africa's Complicated Relationship With It
explainers.summary: The world's permanent court for prosecuting the worst crimes — and why many African governments have accused it of bias.
explainers.tldr: The International Criminal Court (ICC) is a permanent international court that prosecutes individuals for genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity, but has faced sustained criticism, especially from African governments, over a perceived disproportionate focus on African cases.

sections.content: Established in 2002, the ICC is a permanent court, separate from the UN, that prosecutes individuals, not states, for the most serious international crimes when national courts are unable or unwilling to do so themselves. Example: unlike the UN Security Council, the ICC's core mandate focuses specifically on individual criminal responsibility for atrocities.

sections.header: A heavy focus on African cases
sections.content: In its early years, the overwhelming majority of the ICC's formal investigations targeted African leaders and conflicts, fueling accusations that the court disproportionately targets Africa while ignoring comparable crimes by powerful non-African states. Example: several African leaders, including sitting heads of state, have been formally charged by the ICC, a fact often cited by critics as evidence of selective justice.

This perception led some African governments and the African Union to accuse the ICC of neocolonial bias, with a few countries threatening or briefly initiating withdrawal from the court. Example: Burundi formally withdrew from the ICC in 2017, citing these concerns directly.

sections.header: The bigger picture on international justice
sections.content: Defenders of the ICC argue its African caseload partly reflects which countries have accepted its jurisdiction and referred cases to it, rather than deliberate bias, while critics maintain the court still needs to address major power politics limiting its reach elsewhere. Example: major powers like the US, Russia, and China are not full ICC members, meaning their nationals are largely shielded from its jurisdiction, a point frequently raised in this debate.

keyTerms.definition: A permanent court prosecuting individuals for genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity.
Serious violations of the laws and customs of war.

explainers.title: Impeachment, Explained
explainers.summary: The formal process for removing a sitting official from office before their term is up.
explainers.tldr: Impeachment is a formal, usually legislative process for charging a sitting official, often a president, with serious wrongdoing, potentially leading to their removal from office before the end of their term.

sections.content: Impeachment is essentially a formal accusation of serious misconduct against a sitting official, typically initiated and voted on by a legislature, and is a political and legal process rather than a criminal trial in the ordinary sense. Example: in the US system, impeachment by the House of Representatives is only the first step, similar to a criminal indictment, not a final conviction.

Most constitutions define fairly broad grounds for impeachment, often including things like treason, bribery, corruption, or other serious abuses of office, though what specifically counts is often debated and politically contested in practice. Example: the vague nature of many impeachment standards, such as the US Constitution's phrase 'high crimes and misdemeanors,' has fueled ongoing debate about what specifically qualifies.

Being impeached and being removed from office are two separate steps — being impeached typically means being formally charged, while an additional vote, often requiring a higher threshold like a legislative supermajority, is needed to actually remove the official from power. Example: a president can be impeached but still remain in office if the subsequent removal vote fails to reach the required threshold.

keyTerms.definition: The formal process of charging a sitting official with serious wrongdoing.
The separate, often higher-threshold step of actually removing an impeached official.

explainers.title: The African Union's Peace and Security Council
explainers.summary: The AU body responsible for responding to coups, conflicts, and instability across the continent.
explainers.tldr: The African Union's Peace and Security Council is the continent's main body for responding to armed conflicts, coups, and threats to peace, with powers including authorizing peacekeeping missions and suspending member states that experience unconstitutional changes of government.

sections.content: Modeled loosely on the UN Security Council, the AU's Peace and Security Council is responsible for preventing, managing, and resolving conflicts across Africa, including authorizing peace support operations in member states. Example: the Council has authorized AU peacekeeping missions in conflicts including Somalia, aimed at stabilizing the country against extremist insurgent groups.

One of the Council's clearest and most consistently applied tools has been suspending the membership of countries that experience military coups or other unconstitutional changes of government, as a way of formally condemning and pressuring these governments. Example: Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger, and Sudan have all faced AU suspension following recent coups in their countries.

Despite its formal authority, the Council's actual influence is often limited by the AU's reliance on voluntary member state cooperation and funding, meaning its suspensions and calls for action don't always translate into real pressure on the governments involved. Example: several suspended coup governments have continued operating largely unaffected by their AU suspension, since it carries mainly symbolic and diplomatic, rather than direct enforcement, weight.

keyTerms.definition: The AU's main body for responding to conflict and instability across Africa.
A seizure of power outside legal or constitutional means, such as a coup.

explainers.title: The CFA Franc and Monetary Sovereignty in Francophone Africa
explainers.summary: Why many former French colonies still share a currency tied to France, and why critics call it a form of ongoing economic control.
explainers.tldr: The CFA franc, used by 14 mostly former French colonies in West and Central Africa, is pegged to a fixed exchange rate historically guaranteed by France, a system defenders credit with monetary stability but critics argue limits these countries' genuine economic sovereignty.

sections.content: The CFA franc system uses a currency whose value has historically been fixed relative to the French franc, and later the euro, with France historically holding a portion of these countries' foreign reserves and playing a role in the currency's governance. Example: countries using the CFA franc can't independently devalue their currency to respond to their own economic conditions the way countries with fully independent currencies can.

Supporters argue the CFA franc's stability and fixed exchange rate has helped control inflation and provided a predictable currency environment that has encouraged trade and investment in participating countries. Example: CFA franc countries have generally experienced lower average inflation than many neighboring countries with independent currencies.

Critics argue the system perpetuates a form of colonial-era economic dependency, since key monetary decisions remain tied to French oversight, limiting these countries' ability to pursue independent economic policy suited to their own specific needs. Example: critics have specifically pointed to the requirement that a share of these countries' foreign currency reserves be held in French institutions as a lingering symbol of colonial-era control.

In recent years, some CFA franc countries, particularly in West Africa, have pushed for reforms or a full transition to a new independent regional currency, though progress has been slow and contested. Example: West African CFA franc countries have discussed plans for a new currency called the eco, though implementation has repeatedly been delayed.

keyTerms.definition: A currency used by 14 mostly former French colonies, historically pegged and tied to France.
A country's ability to independently control its own currency and monetary policy.

explainers.title: BRICS, Explained
explainers.summary: How a loose grouping of major emerging economies became a symbol of a shifting global order.
explainers.tldr: BRICS, originally Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa, and since expanded to include more countries, is a grouping of major emerging economies that increasingly positions itself as a counterweight to Western-dominated global institutions.

sections.content: The term BRIC was originally coined by an economist to describe Brazil, Russia, India, and China as major rising economies, before South Africa joined and the grouping became a formal diplomatic bloc known as BRICS. Example: the original BRIC countries began holding formal annual summits together starting in 2009.

Rather than shared ideology or political system, BRICS members are united mainly by their status as large, influential emerging economies and a shared interest in having more say in global economic and political institutions historically dominated by Western powers. Example: BRICS countries have pushed for reforms giving emerging economies greater voting power within institutions like the IMF and World Bank.

BRICS has established its own financial institutions, including a New Development Bank, intended to offer developing countries financing alternatives to traditional Western-dominated lenders like the World Bank. Example: the New Development Bank has funded infrastructure projects in member countries as an alternative financing source.

In recent years, BRICS has expanded to include additional countries, reflecting growing interest among emerging and developing economies in aligning with a bloc positioned as an alternative to Western-led global institutions. Example: countries including Egypt, Ethiopia, and Iran have joined or sought to join BRICS as part of this expansion.

keyTerms.definition: A grouping of major emerging economies positioning itself as an alternative to Western-led institutions.
A BRICS-founded financial institution offering an alternative to Western-dominated lenders.

explainers.title: Soft Power vs Hard Power
explainers.summary: The difference between influencing other countries through attraction versus through force or coercion.
explainers.tldr: Hard power is a state's ability to influence others through military force or economic coercion, while soft power is the ability to influence through attraction, culture, and legitimacy, getting others to want what you want rather than forcing them.

sections.content: Hard power relies on tangible, coercive tools — military force, economic sanctions, or the threat of either — to compel other states to act in a particular way. Example: a country imposing trade sanctions to pressure another government into changing a policy is exercising hard power.

Soft power, a term popularized by political scientist Joseph Nye, refers to a country's ability to attract and persuade others through the appeal of its culture, values, and policies, without needing to force compliance. Example: the global popularity of a country's music, films, or universities can help build the kind of goodwill and influence associated with soft power.

Most powerful states rely on a combination of both, using hard power to deter or compel where necessary, while cultivating soft power to build alliances, legitimacy, and long-term influence more cheaply than constant military or economic coercion. Example: a country might fund international scholarship programs or cultural exchanges specifically to build soft power influence among future foreign leaders.

keyTerms.definition: Influence gained through attraction, culture, and legitimacy rather than force.
Influence gained through military force or economic coercion.

explainers.title: Populism, Explained
explainers.summary: Why 'populist' has become one of the most-used and most-contested labels in modern politics.
explainers.tldr: Populism is a political style that frames politics as a struggle between ordinary people and a corrupt or out-of-touch elite, and can appear across the political spectrum, from the political left to the right, unified more by this framing than by any single fixed set of policies.

sections.header: A style more than a fixed ideology
sections.content: Unlike ideologies with a relatively consistent set of policy positions, like socialism or libertarianism, populism is better understood as a political style or strategy that can be attached to very different policy platforms, left-wing or right-wing. Example: some left-wing populist movements focus on economic inequality and corporate power, while right-wing populist movements often focus on immigration and national identity, yet both use similar 'us versus corrupt elites' framing.

Populist movements typically present themselves as the authentic voice of ordinary people against a self-serving, out-of-touch establishment, often bypassing or attacking existing institutions like courts, media, and traditional parties as part of that same corrupt elite. Example: a populist leader might describe career politicians, judges, and journalists as all part of the same out-of-touch establishment blocking the people's true will.

Populism tends to gain traction during periods of economic hardship, rapid social change, or widespread distrust in existing institutions, offering a simple explanation — a corrupt elite is to blame — for complicated problems. Example: populist movements have historically surged following financial crises or periods of rapid, disruptive economic change that leave many people feeling left behind.

Supporters argue populism channels genuine grievances that establishment politics has ignored, while critics warn it can undermine democratic institutions and checks on power by framing any institutional constraint on a popular leader as illegitimate elite obstruction. Example: critics point to populist leaders who, once elected, have moved to weaken courts or media independence by framing them as part of the corrupt elite blocking the people's will.

keyTerms.definition: A political style framing politics as ordinary people versus a corrupt elite.
The existing, often entrenched political and institutional elite in a society.

explainers.title: Neoliberalism, Explained
explainers.summary: The free-market policy approach that reshaped economic policy worldwide from the 1980s onward.
explainers.tldr: Neoliberalism refers to a policy approach favoring free markets, deregulation, privatization, and reduced government intervention in the economy, which became highly influential in global economic policy from the 1980s onward.

sections.content: Neoliberal policy typically favors reducing government regulation of business, privatizing state-owned industries, cutting trade barriers, and generally shrinking the direct role of government in managing the economy. Example: privatizing a previously state-owned telecommunications or airline company reflects a classic neoliberal policy move.

Neoliberal policies gained major influence starting in the 1980s, associated with leaders like Margaret Thatcher in the UK and Ronald Reagan in the US, and were later widely promoted to developing countries through international financial institutions. Example: structural adjustment programs required by institutions like the IMF often pushed developing countries toward neoliberal reforms, like reducing subsidies and privatizing state industries, in exchange for loans.

Supporters credit neoliberal reforms with boosting economic growth, efficiency, and global trade integration, while critics argue the same policies have often deepened inequality and weakened public services and worker protections. Example: critics point to increased income inequality in many countries that adopted extensive neoliberal reforms as evidence the benefits weren't evenly shared.

keyTerms.definition: A policy approach favoring free markets, deregulation, and privatization.
Economic reforms required by lenders like the IMF in exchange for loans.

explainers.title: Ubuntu: An African Political Philosophy
explainers.summary: The southern African philosophy of shared humanity that has directly shaped modern political reconciliation efforts.
explainers.tldr: Ubuntu, a concept from southern African philosophy often summarized as 'I am because we are,' emphasizes shared humanity and interconnectedness over individualism, and has directly influenced political approaches to justice and reconciliation, most notably in post-apartheid South Africa.

sections.content: Ubuntu holds that a person's humanity is fundamentally bound up with their relationships to others, meaning individual identity and dignity can't be fully separated from the wellbeing of the wider community. Example: the phrase 'I am because we are' captures this idea that individual identity is defined through connection to others, not purely through individual achievement.

Applied to politics and governance, Ubuntu philosophy tends to emphasize collective wellbeing, consensus-building, and restorative approaches to conflict over purely individualistic or purely punitive approaches. Example: Ubuntu-influenced governance ideas favor resolving conflicts in ways that restore relationships within the community, rather than focusing solely on punishing wrongdoers.

Ubuntu philosophy directly influenced South Africa's post-apartheid Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which prioritized public truth-telling and reconciliation over purely punitive justice for apartheid-era crimes. Example: Archbishop Desmond Tutu, who led the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, explicitly invoked Ubuntu philosophy to explain the commission's approach of favoring restorative justice over pure retribution.

keyTerms.definition: A southern African philosophy emphasizing shared humanity and interconnectedness.
An approach to justice focused on repairing harm and relationships rather than pure punishment.

explainers.title: Lobbying and Think Tanks: Influence Outside Elected Office
explainers.summary: How organizations without a single elected official can still shape major political decisions.
explainers.tldr: Lobbying and think tanks are two of the main ways organized interests and ideas influence government policy outside of formal elections, with lobbyists directly pressing officials on specific policies and think tanks shaping the broader ideas and research that inform policy debates.

sections.content: Lobbying is the practice of individuals or organizations directly engaging with lawmakers or officials to influence specific legislation, regulations, or government decisions in their favor. Example: an industry association might lobby lawmakers directly to shape the specific wording of a new regulation affecting their business.

Lobbying is practiced by an enormously wide range of interests, from large corporations and industry groups to labor unions and nonprofit advocacy organizations, each seeking to shape policy in line with their particular interests or values. Example: environmental advocacy groups lobby for stronger environmental regulations, just as energy companies often lobby for the opposite.

Think tanks are research organizations that produce policy analysis and recommendations, often shaping the intellectual and ideological framing that lawmakers and the public use to think about a given issue, rather than lobbying on specific bills directly. Example: a think tank's research report on a proposed policy can shape how journalists, officials, and the public understand and debate that policy's likely effects.

Critics argue that lobbying and think tank funding can give wealthy interests disproportionate influence over policy compared to ordinary citizens, particularly when funding sources for research or lobbying efforts aren't fully transparent. Example: debates over campaign finance and lobbying disclosure rules are largely driven by concerns about this kind of outsized, sometimes hidden, influence.

keyTerms.definition: Direct engagement with lawmakers to influence specific legislation or policy.
A research organization producing policy analysis and shaping policy debates.

explainers.title: Disinformation and Propaganda in the Internet Age
explainers.summary: How social media has transformed the speed, scale, and difficulty of controlling political propaganda.
explainers.tldr: The internet and social media have dramatically increased the speed and reach at which political disinformation can spread, making propaganda and manipulation campaigns more difficult to detect and contain than in earlier eras of mass media.

sections.content: Disinformation refers to false information spread deliberately to deceive, while misinformation refers to false information spread without necessarily intending to deceive — a distinction that matters for understanding motive even though both can cause real harm. Example: someone deliberately creating a fake news story to influence an election is spreading disinformation, while someone unknowingly sharing that same false story is spreading misinformation.

sections.header: Why social media changed the game
sections.content: Social media platforms allow false or misleading content to spread extremely quickly and cheaply across borders, often outpacing the ability of journalists, platforms, or governments to correct it before real damage is done. Example: a fabricated political claim can reach millions of people within hours on social media, far faster than a traditional newspaper correction could ever spread.

Some governments run deliberate disinformation campaigns targeting foreign elections or public opinion, using networks of fake accounts and coordinated messaging to spread confusion or specific political narratives. Example: investigations into foreign interference in various national elections have identified coordinated social media campaigns designed to spread misleading political content.

Efforts to combat disinformation, including content moderation and fact-checking, face genuine tension with concerns about free speech and who gets to decide what counts as false or misleading, making this one of the more difficult ongoing challenges in modern political communication. Example: debates over how aggressively social media platforms should moderate political content reflect this unresolved tension between limiting harm and protecting free expression.

keyTerms.definition: False information deliberately spread to deceive.
False information spread without necessarily intending to deceive.
